To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
type III IFN prevents influenza virus spread to the lower respiratory tract and limits virus transmission.
IFN-λ is a key factor that prevents virus spread from the nasal cavity to the lungs and that IFN-α and IFN-λ have different functions in the respiratory tract.
type III interferon has an important function in the upper respiratory tract and that it prevents the transmission of respiratory infections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and characterization of a new model of influenza virus transmission, which allows us to study host factors that restrict the spread of respiratory viruses.
the role of type III IFN in the control of influenza virus transmission.
the development of novel strategies to prevent transmission of influenza virus and possibly other respiratory viruses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IFN-λ is the key cytokine in the respiratory tract that protects against influenza virus transmission.
type I and type 3 IFN have non-redundent roles in restricting virus spread in the upper respiratory tract and that the type III IFN is the most important IFN in limiting virus transmission.

the antiviral activity of IFN-λ is superior compared with IFN-β in the upper airway and that the combination of IFN-α and IFN-β has an additive antiviral activity in the lower airway, but not in the upper air.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IFN-λ receptor is the most important host factor for limiting the spread of a respiratory virus from the nose to the lungs, which in turn greatly reduces transmission to naïve hosts.

IFN-λ is the major antiviral cytokine in the upper airway mucosa that prevents virus transmission to naïve contacts, whereas IFN-α is the major antitumor cytokine in the lower respiratory tract that limits the spread of virus from the upper airway.
IFN-λ plays a key role in limiting the dissemination of respiratory viruses from the nose to the lungs and in blocking virus transmission to contacts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
type III interferon is essential for preventing virus transmission and that it does so by limiting virus replication in the upper airway.
type III IFNs, but not type I IFNs, play a decisive role in the upper airway and prevent virus spread from the nose to the lungs and limit virus transmission.
IFN-λ plays an important role in limiting the spread of influenza virus from the nose to the lungs and in reducing virus transmission from infected to naïve mice.
